  1. 1 Must see within Punggol

    Coney Island Park (Pulau Serangoon)

    A 133-hectare island off Punggol, once owned by the Aw brothers of Tiger Balm. In 1950 it was sold to a businessman who planned a resort modelled on New York's Coney Island. Since October 2015 a 50-hectare NParks park has kept it deliberately rustic: casuarina woods, a 2.5 km car-free trail, hidden beaches and bridges at both ends to the mainland.

    Look for Open 7am–7pm, free

    Coney Island, Punggol, Singapore (West entrance off Punggol Promenade / East entrance off Pasir Ris side; to confirm at geocode)

    Recommended by , , +2, ,

  2. 2 Must see within Punggol

    Punggol Beach Massacre Site

    A National Heritage Board historic site. On 23 February 1942, during the Japanese Sook Ching operation, a Hojo Kempei firing squad killed some 300–400 Chinese civilians on the Punggol foreshore. Human remains turned up in the sand in 1977 and 1997. An NHB marker set up in 1995, for the 50th anniversary of the end of WWII, records the killings.

    Look for Open-air memorial marker, free

    Punggol Point foreshore (Punggol Point Park), Punggol, Singapore

    Recommended by , , +1,

  3. 3 Must see within Punggol

    Punggol Waterway Park

    The 4.2-km park along Singapore's longest man-made waterway, in four themed zones (Nature Cove, Recreation Zone, Heritage Zone on Old Punggol Road, Green Gallery) linked by five photogenic bridges — the dome-shaped Jewel Bridge for sunsets over the Punggol and Serangoon reservoirs, the snaking red Sunrise Bridge at the eastern Sunrise Gateway, plus the Wave, Adventure and Kelong bridges. Otters are regulars.

    Look for Free; best at sunrise (east) and sunset (Jewel Bridge, west)

    Punggol Waterway (Sentul Crescent / Punggol Central), Punggol, Singapore

    Recommended by , , +1,

    Kwang Kee Teochew Fish Porridge (One Punggol)

    Punggol branch of a Teochew fish-porridge stall founded in 1962 and on the MICHELIN Bib Gourmand list every year since 2021. Known for a light, clean, sweet-savoury broth and fresh fish slices; the original is at Newton Food Centre.

    One Punggol Hawker Centre, #02-19, Punggol, Singapore (street + postal to confirm at geocode)

  9. 9 Worth the detour within Punggol

    Punggol Point Park

    A seafront park at the northern tip of Punggol, opened on 20 November 2011 at the old Punggol Point fishing-village beach. People come for the sunset over the Strait of Johor, the jetty views across to Malaysia, and the WWII Sook Ching memorial on its foreshore.

    Look for Open 24h, free

    Punggol Point Road, Punggol, Singapore

    Recommended by , ,

  10. 10 Worth the detour within Punggol

    Punggol Digital District (SIT Punggol Campus)

    Singapore's first 'enterprise district' (~50 ha, phase 1 opened from Q3 2024), marketed as Singapore's "Silicon Valley" and built around the Singapore Institute of Technology's new Punggol campus (classes from Sept 2024); the BCA Green Mark Platinum campus runs on 20,000+ sensors and smart lamp-posts. Campus Heart houses the SIT Visitor Gallery.

    Look for SIT Visitor Gallery; pair with Punggol Coast Hawker Centre

    Punggol Coast, Punggol Way, Singapore (beside Punggol Coast MRT)

    Recommended by , ,

  13. 13 Worth the detour within Punggol

    Matilda House

    One of Singapore's oldest houses: a 1902 single-storey tropical bungalow built for Alexander Cashin and named for his mother Josephine Matilda — the Cashins being the Eurasian family whose patriarch became Singapore's first Eurasian millionaire. Conserved by URA in Feb 2000 and restored (façade and interior) as the clubhouse of the 'A Treasure Trove' condominium in 2015; view from Punggol Walk.

    Look for Conserved 1902 bungalow; condo clubhouse — exterior view only

    78 Punggol Walk, Singapore

    Recommended by ,

  20. 20 Worth the detour within Punggol · Chinese

    Lao Jiang Superior Soup (Oasis Terraces)

    A homegrown soup specialist since 2011: a sweet-savoury, light seafood broth loaded with prawns, fish maw, pork slices, abalone slices and beancurd-skin fish sticks, over rice, hor fun or you mian — with an addictive chilli and fresh lard. Featured by Eatbook (Punggol guide) and reviewed by Seth Lui.

    Punggol East Container Park (Tebing Lane)

    An Artbox-style cluster of shipping-container eateries, a roller-skating rink and plant nurseries next to the Social Innovation Park, where the Riverside Walk meets Tebing Lane's cafés — the casual evening hangout of Punggol East (Daniel Food Diary, TheSmartLocal, Little Day Out, Sassy Mama).

  23. 23 Deep cut within Punggol

    Masjid Al-Islah

    Punggol's only mosque (2015, capacity 4,000), designed by Formwerkz Architects as an 'open mosque': a porous, naturally ventilated village cluster of prayer hall, school and offices around landscaped courts — widely published as a model of contemporary Singapore mosque architecture.

    Look for Visitors welcome outside prayer times; dress modestly

    30 Punggol Field, Singapore 828812

    Recommended by , ,

  24. 24 Deep cut within Punggol

    Oasis Terraces

    HDB's new-generation neighbourhood centre on the Punggol Waterway (opened 2018–19), designed by Serie Architects with Multiply Architects as a stepped garden of terraces cascading to the water, with a rooftop community garden and polyclinic — published internationally by Dezeen and designboom. Houses Lao Jiang Superior Soup and Rise & Grind.

    Look for Free; climb the terraces to the rooftop garden for waterway views

    681 Punggol Drive, Singapore 820681

How we choose

Every place is recommended by named sources (review-aggregator star ratings never count as the recommender), pinned to its door from a published coordinate, and status-checked. Closed places stay, flagged, so you know they’re gone.

Must see
The places to plan a visit around — graded within each area, not across the city.
Worth the detour
Strong picks, worth going out of your way for.
Deep cut
For the curious: smaller, odder, more local.

Within each area, places are ordered by tier, then by number of named sources — never by popularity. Numbers on the cards match the pins on the map. No ratings, prices or opening hours are shown, because the guide doesn’t hold verified ones.
